title: Rockvale Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Rockvale wells have a 51-foot median depth, but fractured bedrock can make drilling costs and water production vary sharply.
h1: Rockvale, Colorado well depth, yield, and drilling costs
intro_html:
Buying land or a home near Rockvale means looking past the average well. Permits within 5 miles show a median well depth of 51 feet, but the recorded range reaches 1,870 feet. Most reported yields are usable, with a median of 6.0 gallons per minute, yet the local ground is fractured mountain bedrock, so nearby wells are a starting point rather than a guarantee.

This page uses Colorado Division of Water Resources permit records for Rockvale and nearby Williamsburg, Florence, Brookside, Lincoln Park, Cañon City, and Park Center. The records can help with budgeting and due diligence, but a driller still needs to evaluate the specific lot, access, geology, casing, grout, pump, and electrical requirements.

sections.heading: Rockvale well depth depends on the bedrock
sections.html:
Rockvale’s recorded median well depth is 51 feet, and the middle half of wells falls from 35 to 120 feet. That sounds shallow, but it does not describe every lot. The 90th-percentile depth is 417 feet, and the deepest recorded well is 1,870 feet. Depth records also show that 71% of wells are under 100 feet, while 13% fall from 100 to 300 feet, 11% from 300 to 600 feet, and 4% exceed 600 feet.

For a drilling bid, use the median as a local reference, not a promise. Fractured granite and gneiss can carry water in narrow zones, so one neighbor’s shallow success may not repeat across the road. Ask for a written estimate that explains footage, casing, grout, pump work, and what happens if the hole must go deeper.

sections.heading: What Rockvale wells produce
sections.html:
Among the Rockvale-area permits that report pump yield, the median is 6.0 gallons per minute. The middle half runs from 3.5 to 10.8 gallons per minute. Half of the reported wells produce from 5 to 15 gallons per minute, while 28% produce from 1 to 5 gallons per minute. Only 3% are under 1 gallon per minute, and 18% report more than 15 gallons per minute.

Those figures describe well production, not unlimited household use. A 1-gallon-per-minute well may work with adequate storage and conservative demand, but it leaves less margin for irrigation, livestock, guests, or leaks. Confirm the permitted use and ask for the driller’s yield test, recovery information, and pump-storage design before treating the reported median as your expected supply.

sections.heading: Rockvale water levels and the local trend
sections.html:
Only 41 wells in the records report a static water level, so the water-level sample is much smaller than the depth sample. Within those measurements, the median depth to water is 70 feet, and the middle half ranges from 22 to 100 feet below the surface.

The decade figures move from a 60-foot median in the 2010s to 75 feet in the 2020s. That is a deeper reported water level in the newer decade, but the limited number of measurements means it should not be treated as proof of a broad water-table decline. Static levels vary with location, season, pumping history, and measurement conditions. Have the existing well measured under comparable conditions, and ask whether the level recovers after pumping.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Rockvale, and when
sections.html:
Permit activity around Rockvale is not new. Records show 6 permits from the 1950s, 17 from the 1960s, 64 from the 1970s, 128 from the 1980s, 397 from the 1990s, 192 from the 2000s, 151 from the 2010s, and 58 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. Of 1,235 permits, 871 are recorded as constructed.

The most active drillers named in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 317 wells; Arkansas Valley Drilling (Moore, Todd A.), with 107; and Finney Drilling (Finney, Larry D.), with 69. These records show local experience, not an endorsement. Verify current licensing, insurance, references, and availability, then compare the proposed construction details rather than choosing only by the lowest bid.

sections.heading: Rockvale drilling cost at typical local depth
sections.html:
The cost model for Rockvale assumes fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. The typical drilling rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 51-foot median depth, the drilled hole models at about $3,300 to $5,100. A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical models at about $9,300 to $17,100.

That finished range is a planning figure, not a guaranteed contract price. A hole reaching the deeper part of the local record can change the budget substantially, and difficult access, casing, grout, surface conditions, power distance, or low production can add work. Get the bid broken into drilling, casing, grout, development, pump, tank, trenching, electrical, testing, and permit-related items.

sections.heading: Rockvale risks to check before closing or building
sections.html:
Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer: 1,197 wells do so. Only 15 name an alluvial aquifer and 6 name the Dakota Sandstone; no wells in this dataset name a Denver Basin aquifer. That makes local well history especially important. Review construction records, pump tests, water quality results, and any history of low yield, dry holes, or repairs.

Environmental screening also deserves attention. Within about 10 miles are 33 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 88 historic mine features, and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Their presence does not establish contamination at a particular parcel. Test the existing or new well through a qualified laboratory, and place septic, wells, driveways, and building areas with groundwater flow, setbacks, access, and future maintenance in mind.

sections.heading: A practical Rockvale plan for buying or building
sections.html:
Before buying near Rockvale, obtain the DWR permit, construction report, pump-yield information, static water level, well test, and recent laboratory results. Compare several nearby records in Williamsburg, Florence, Brookside, Lincoln Park, Cañon City, or Park Center, but give the greatest weight to wells with similar elevation, geology, and lot conditions. A nearby well can improve your estimate without proving what your parcel will produce.

For a vacant lot, confirm legal water supply, permitted household use, septic feasibility, access for a large drilling rig, and the location of power and trench runs before closing. If the basin is over-appropriated, ask Colorado water counsel or the permitting authority whether an augmentation plan is needed. Plan storage and conservation around the tested yield, and keep a contingency for deeper drilling or a low-producing hole.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Rockvale, Colorado?
faq.a: Rockvale-area records show a median well depth of 51 feet, with the middle half from 35 to 120 feet. However, the 90th-percentile depth is 417 feet and the deepest recorded well is 1,870 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss make depth vary sharply from one parcel to another, so nearby construction reports are more useful than the median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Rockvale?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $65 to $100 per foot for fractured mountain bedrock. At the 51-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $3,300 to $5,100. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $9,300 to $17,100. Deeper drilling, access, casing, grout, and low production can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Rockvale wells produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a 6.0-gallon-per-minute median, with the middle half from 3.5 to 10.8 gallons per minute. Half of reported wells fall from 5 to 15 gallons per minute. The yield records cover 214 wells, so request the actual test and recovery information for the property rather than relying only on the area statistic.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Rockvale, Colorado?
faq.a: Permit records do not establish that a particular well is safe to drink. The area includes 33 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 88 historic mine features, and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Test the property’s water through a qualified laboratory, especially for contaminants relevant to the site’s geology and nearby environmental history.

faq.q: Are Rockvale wells getting deeper or losing water?
faq.a: The 41 wells reporting static water levels have a median depth to water of 70 feet, with the middle half from 22 to 100 feet. The decade median changes from 60 feet in the 2010s to 75 feet in the 2020s. That suggests deeper reported levels in the newer measurements, but the small sample does not prove a region-wide decline.
